label: Signs of Severe Dehydration: Go to Hospital Immediately
text: Condition: Acute Diarrhea and Dehydration. Section: Signs of Severe Dehydration: Go to Hospital Immediately. Lethargy or unconsciousness. Sunken eyes. Not able to drink at all, or drinking very poorly. Skin pinch test: pinch the skin on the abdomen, if the skin goes back very slowly (takes more than 2 seconds to flatten), this indicates severe dehydration. Very rapid or weak pulse. Very low blood pressure. Rapid breathing. Passing many watery stools very frequently with no improvement. Repeated vomiting preventing any fluid intake. Blood in stools with no improvement after 2 days of treatment. Diarrhea with high fever and worsening general condition. Diarrhea in a person with severe malnutrition or known HIV. Persistent diarrhea lasting more than 14 days with signs of dehydration or serious illness.
source_title: Standard Treatment Workflow (STW) for the Management of Acute Diarrhea
source_publisher: Department of Health Research, Ministry of Health and Family Welfare, Government of India

label: Self-Care at Home: Fluid Replacement is the Most Important Step
text: Condition: Acute Diarrhea and Dehydration. Section: Self-Care at Home: Fluid Replacement is the Most Important Step. Start oral rehydration immediately, the most important treatment for diarrhea at home is replacing lost fluids and salts. Use ORS (Oral Rehydration Salt) sachets available at any pharmacy or government health centre: dissolve one sachet in the amount of clean water shown on the packet (usually 200 ml or 1 litre) and sip frequently. If ORS sachets are not available, a homemade alternative can be used temporarily: add a pinch of salt and a small amount of sugar to a glass of clean water, stir well, and sip frequently. Other suitable homemade fluids: salted rice water, salted yogurt drink (lassi with salt), vegetable or chicken soup with salt, unsweetened fresh fruit juice, coconut water. Give extra fluids after each loose stool, adults should drink at least 200 ml after each episode. Unsuitable fluids that worsen diarrhea: carbonated beverages (cold drinks/soda), commercial sweetened fruit juices, sweetened tea or coffee.
source_title: Standard Treatment Workflow (STW) for the Management of Acute Diarrhea
source_publisher: Department of Health Research, Ministry of Health and Family Welfare, Government of India

label: Self-Care at Home: Fluid Replacement is the Most Important Step
text: Condition: Acute Diarrhea and Dehydration. Section: Self-Care at Home: Fluid Replacement is the Most Important Step. Continue eating, do not fast. Eat light, easily digestible foods. Avoid oily or spicy food during illness. Wash hands thoroughly with soap and water before eating, after using the toilet, and after handling stool. Use clean, safe drinking water only, boil water if safety is uncertain. Return for medical attention immediately if: passing many watery stools, repeatedly vomiting, unable to drink, developing fever, noticing blood in stool, or condition is not improving in 5 days.
source_title: Standard Treatment Workflow (STW) for the Management of Acute Diarrhea
source_publisher: Department of Health Research, Ministry of Health and Family Welfare, Government of India

label: See a Doctor
text: Condition: Acute Diarrhea and Dehydration. Section: See a Doctor. Diarrhea not improving after 5 days of home management. Any blood in the stools (dysentery). Significant vomiting along with diarrhea making it hard to keep fluids down. Signs of moderate dehydration: restlessness, sunken eyes, feeling very thirsty, skin pinch goes back slowly. Fever along with diarrhea. Diarrhea in a person with diabetes, heart disease, or kidney disease. Diarrhea lasting more than 14 days (persistent diarrhea). Diarrhea after travel to a new place or after eating outside food with suspected contamination.
source_title: Standard Treatment Workflow (STW) for the Management of Acute Diarrhea
source_publisher: Department of Health Research, Ministry of Health and Family Welfare, Government of India

label: Go to Hospital Without Delay
text: Condition: Acute Diarrhea and Dehydration. Section: Go to Hospital Without Delay. Any sign of severe dehydration listed above, unconsciousness, unable to drink, skin pinch very slow, very weak pulse. Blood in stools with no improvement after 2 days of treatment. Persistent diarrhea (more than 14 days) with dehydration or serious infection signs. Diarrhea with severe vomiting and complete inability to keep fluids down. Suspected cholera: sudden onset of very profuse watery diarrhea (rice-water stool), especially in an area with known cholera.
source_title: Standard Treatment Workflow (STW) for the Management of Acute Diarrhea
source_publisher: Department of Health Research, Ministry of Health and Family Welfare, Government of India

label: Condition Overview
text: Condition: Acute Diarrhea and Dehydration. Section: Condition Overview. Diarrhea means three or more loose or watery stools per day. Acute diarrhea lasts less than 14 days. Diarrhea lasting more than 14 days is persistent diarrhea. Dysentery means blood is present in the stools.
source_title: Standard Treatment Workflow (STW) for the Management of Acute Diarrhea
source_publisher: Department of Health Research, Ministry of Health and Family Welfare, Government of India

label: Simple Home Dehydration Check (Skin Pinch Test)
text: Condition: Acute Diarrhea and Dehydration. Section: Simple Home Dehydration Check (Skin Pinch Test). Pinch the skin on the abdomen between two fingers, hold for one second, then let go. Watch how quickly it returns to normal: if it goes back immediately, no significant dehydration; if it stays raised for a brief instant, some dehydration, needs ORS urgently; if it goes back very slowly, taking more than 2 seconds, severe dehydration, go to hospital immediately.
source_title: Standard Treatment Workflow (STW) for the Management of Acute Diarrhea
source_publisher: Department of Health Research, Ministry of Health and Family Welfare, Government of India

condition: Acute Respiratory Infections (Cough, Cold, Bronchitis, Pneumonia)
label: Signs of Respiratory Failure: Call 112 or Go to Hospital Immediately
text: Condition: Acute Respiratory Infections (Cough, Cold, Bronchitis, Pneumonia). Section: Signs of Respiratory Failure: Call 112 or Go to Hospital Immediately. Breathing rate above 30 breaths per minute. Breathing with the belly moving opposite to the chest (abdominal-thoracic paradox), a sign of severe breathing difficulty. Blue or purple colour on the lips, fingertips, or face (cyanosis), indicates critically low oxygen. Only able to speak a few words at a time due to breathlessness. Oxygen saturation at or below 92% in a person aged 50 or below, or below 90% in a person over 50. Confusion or disorientation along with breathing problems. Coughing up blood (frank haemoptysis), may also suggest TB or a more serious condition. Very low blood pressure combined with breathing difficulty. Very high or very low body temperature alongside breathing difficulty. Suspected flu with breathing difficulty, especially if there is a history of recent travel or an ongoing flu epidemic.
source_title: Standard Treatment Workflow (STW) for Management of Acute Respiratory Infection in Adults
source_publisher: Department of Health Research, Ministry of Health and Family Welfare, Government of India

condition: Acute Respiratory Infections (Cough, Cold, Bronchitis, Pneumonia)
label: Self-Care at Home for Mild Upper Respiratory Infection or Mild Bronchitis
text: Condition: Acute Respiratory Infections (Cough, Cold, Bronchitis, Pneumonia). Section: Self-Care at Home for Mild Upper Respiratory Infection or Mild Bronchitis. Rest and stay home away from others to avoid spreading the infection. Drink plenty of fluids, water, warm soups, warm water with honey and ginger, coconut water. Paracetamol can be taken for fever or body aches as per the dosage on the pack. Steam inhalation can help relieve nasal and chest congestion. Warm salt water gargling helps relieve throat discomfort. Avoid smoking and exposure to smoke or dust. Avoid cold beverages and cold environments. Viral upper respiratory infections (common cold) do not benefit from antibiotics, do not self-medicate with antibiotics. Most mild colds and coughs in a healthy adult resolve within 7 to 10 days without medication.
source_title: Standard Treatment Workflow (STW) for Management of Acute Respiratory Infection in Adults
source_publisher: Department of Health Research, Ministry of Health and Family Welfare, Government of India

condition: Acute Respiratory Infections (Cough, Cold, Bronchitis, Pneumonia)
label: See a Doctor
text: Condition: Acute Respiratory Infections (Cough, Cold, Bronchitis, Pneumonia). Section: See a Doctor. Cough lasting more than 10 to 14 days without improvement. Fever that is persistent, high, or accompanied by chills. Cough producing yellow, green, or blood-tinged sputum. Chest pain that worsens with breathing or coughing. Significant breathlessness during light activity or at rest. Cough or cold with wheezing (whistling sound in chest). Sore throat with high fever and swollen neck glands. Any respiratory illness in a person with diabetes, heart disease, chronic lung disease, or kidney disease, these are high-risk groups. Cough with night sweats, unexplained weight loss, or prolonged fatigue, these may be signs of TB. Symptoms that started improving but then got significantly worse.
source_title: Standard Treatment Workflow (STW) for Management of Acute Respiratory Infection in Adults
source_publisher: Department of Health Research, Ministry of Health and Family Welfare, Government of India

condition: Acute Respiratory Infections (Cough, Cold, Bronchitis, Pneumonia)
label: Go to Hospital Without Delay
text: Condition: Acute Respiratory Infections (Cough, Cold, Bronchitis, Pneumonia). Section: Go to Hospital Without Delay. Any danger sign listed above, breathing rate above 30, blue lips, inability to speak, confusion, coughing blood. Oxygen saturation at or below 92%. Suspected pneumonia in a person aged 65 or above, or with confusion, low blood pressure, or fast breathing. Suspected epidemic flu with breathing difficulty. No improvement after 2 to 3 days of treatment for bronchitis or a prescribed antibiotic course.
source_title: Standard Treatment Workflow (STW) for Management of Acute Respiratory Infection in Adults
source_publisher: Department of Health Research, Ministry of Health and Family Welfare, Government of India

condition: Acute Respiratory Infections (Cough, Cold, Bronchitis, Pneumonia)
label: Types Covered
text: Condition: Acute Respiratory Infections (Cough, Cold, Bronchitis, Pneumonia). Section: Types Covered. Acute Upper Respiratory Infection (common cold, catarrh). Acute Bronchitis. Community Acquired Pneumonia (CAP).
source_title: Standard Treatment Workflow (STW) for Management of Acute Respiratory Infection in Adults
source_publisher: Department of Health Research, Ministry of Health and Family Welfare, Government of India

label: Red Flag Signs: Go to Hospital Immediately
text: Condition: Acute Rhinosinusitis (Sinus Infection). Section: Red Flag Signs: Go to Hospital Immediately. Swelling or redness around the eye, or eye being pushed forward (proptosis), indicates the infection has spread to the eye socket. Double vision or significant vision disturbance. Altered mental state or confusion, indicates the infection may have spread to the brain. Severe headache with stiff neck, may indicate meningitis. Increasing swelling or fullness on the forehead. Facial skin, palate, or inner nasal tissues turning dark or discoloured, suggests invasive fungal sinusitis, which is a medical emergency, especially in diabetic patients. Facial numbness or reduced sensation on the face. Signs of sinusitis in a person with diabetes or on immunosuppressive treatment, these individuals are at high risk of a rapidly worsening infection.
source_title: Standard Treatment Workflow (STW) for the Management of Acute Rhinosinusitis
source_publisher: Department of Health Research, Ministry of Health and Family Welfare, Government of India

label: Self-Care at Home for Mild Sinusitis
text: Condition: Acute Rhinosinusitis (Sinus Infection). Section: Self-Care at Home for Mild Sinusitis. Rinse the nose with normal saline nasal wash, dissolve a pinch of salt in a cup of clean water and gently rinse each nostril. This helps clear mucus and improves breathing. Steam inhalation for 10 to 15 minutes, two or three sessions a day, can relieve nasal congestion. Drink adequate fluids to keep mucus thin and easier to drain. Sleep with your head slightly elevated to help drainage. Avoid smoking and exposure to tobacco smoke, dust, and strong chemical smells. Symptoms lasting less than 7 days after a cold are usually viral and self-limiting, rest, fluids, and saline nasal wash are appropriate. Do not use nasal decongestant sprays for more than 3 to 5 days, prolonged use can worsen nasal congestion. Address dental hygiene, untreated upper tooth decay can cause sinus infection on that side.
source_title: Standard Treatment Workflow (STW) for the Management of Acute Rhinosinusitis
source_publisher: Department of Health Research, Ministry of Health and Family Welfare, Government of India

label: See a Doctor
text: Condition: Acute Rhinosinusitis (Sinus Infection). Section: See a Doctor. Nasal blockage, nasal discharge, or facial pressure or pain lasting more than 7 days after a cold. Thick yellow or green nasal discharge with fever. Pain or pressure over the cheeks, forehead, or between the eyes. Reduced or absent sense of smell. Symptoms not improving after a full course of prescribed antibiotics. Recurrent sinusitis episodes (more than once in a few months). Sinusitis in a person with diabetes, they must see a doctor promptly given higher risk of severe infection. Sinusitis with suspected dental origin, pain on one side of the face near upper teeth.
source_title: Standard Treatment Workflow (STW) for the Management of Acute Rhinosinusitis
source_publisher: Department of Health Research, Ministry of Health and Family Welfare, Government of India

label: Go to Hospital Without Delay
text: Condition: Acute Rhinosinusitis (Sinus Infection). Section: Go to Hospital Without Delay. Any red flag sign listed above, eye swelling, double vision, confusion, stiff neck, forehead fullness, dark facial tissue. Suspected invasive fungal sinusitis in a diabetic or immunocompromised person. No improvement after 10 days of correctly prescribed antibiotic treatment. Worsening symptoms while already on antibiotic treatment.
source_title: Standard Treatment Workflow (STW) for the Management of Acute Rhinosinusitis
source_publisher: Department of Health Research, Ministry of Health and Family Welfare, Government of India

label: Condition Overview
text: Condition: Acute Rhinosinusitis (Sinus Infection). Section: Condition Overview. Sinusitis is suspected when nasal blockage, nasal discharge, or facial pain lasting more than 7 days follows a cold. Symptoms lasting less than 7 days are usually a viral cold and do not need antibiotics.
source_title: Standard Treatment Workflow (STW) for the Management of Acute Rhinosinusitis
source_publisher: Department of Health Research, Ministry of Health and Family Welfare, Government of India

label: Red Flag Signs: Seek Emergency Care Immediately
text: Condition: Bacterial Skin Infections. Section: Red Flag Signs: Seek Emergency Care Immediately. Fever above 100.4 degrees Fahrenheit. Heart rate above 90 beats per minute. Breathing rate above 24 breaths per minute. Very high white blood cell count (signs of sepsis). Severe pain in the skin followed by a sudden, deceptive absence of pain, this may indicate necrotising fasciitis, a life-threatening infection. Dark discoloration of the overlying skin. Skin blistering, sloughing (peeling off), or tissue breakdown. Low blood pressure or signs of shock.
source_title: Standard Treatment Workflow (STW) for Bacterial Skin Infections
source_publisher: Department of Health Research, Ministry of Health and Family Welfare, Government of India

label: Danger Signs in Staphylococcal Scalded Skin Syndrome
text: Condition: Bacterial Skin Infections. Section: Danger Signs in Staphylococcal Scalded Skin Syndrome. Widespread peeling or scaling of skin across the body. Skin that appears tender and warm before it starts to peel. Fever with general feeling of being very unwell. Signs of dehydration.
source_title: Standard Treatment Workflow (STW) for Bacterial Skin Infections
source_publisher: Department of Health Research, Ministry of Health and Family Welfare, Government of India

label: General Self-Care at Home
text: Condition: Bacterial Skin Infections. Section: General Self-Care at Home. Maintain good skin hygiene and wash hands regularly. Avoid applying oil on affected skin. Eat adequate nutritious food to support healing. For small wounds or minor folliculitis, keep the area clean and dry. Do not squeeze, pick, or burst a boil or abscess, this can spread the infection. Wash clothes and towels separately in hot water and dry them in sunlight. Avoid sharing towels, clothes, or personal items with others.
source_title: Standard Treatment Workflow (STW) for Bacterial Skin Infections
source_publisher: Department of Health Research, Ministry of Health and Family Welfare, Government of India

label: See a Doctor Within 1 to 2 Days
text: Condition: Bacterial Skin Infections. Section: See a Doctor Within 1 to 2 Days. A boil, abscess, or skin swelling that is growing larger, becoming more painful, or not improving. Redness spreading outward from a wound or infection site. Any skin infection with mild fever. Skin infection in a person with diabetes, skin infections tend to be more severe in diabetic patients. Recurrent boils or folliculitis in multiple family members. Infection affecting the lower limbs with redness, pain, and swelling (cellulitis). A thick black crust with an underlying sore (ecthyma). Impetigo (wet yellow-brown crusts over inflamed skin) that is widespread or not improving.
source_title: Standard Treatment Workflow (STW) for Bacterial Skin Infections
source_publisher: Department of Health Research, Ministry of Health and Family Welfare, Government of India

label: Go to Hospital Without Delay
text: Condition: Bacterial Skin Infections. Section: Go to Hospital Without Delay. Any red flag sign listed above, fever, fast heartbeat, fast breathing, low blood pressure. Severe pain followed by sudden relief, possible necrotising fasciitis. Dark skin over an infected area. Widespread skin peeling or blistering. A skin infection in someone who is immunocompromised (on steroids, chemotherapy, or with HIV). A large abscess or carbuncle that requires drainage. No improvement after 2 to 3 days of treatment. Signs of blood poisoning (septicaemia): high fever, confusion, rapid deterioration.
source_title: Standard Treatment Workflow (STW) for Bacterial Skin Infections
source_publisher: Department of Health Research, Ministry of Health and Family Welfare, Government of India

label: Types Covered
text: Condition: Bacterial Skin Infections. Section: Types Covered. Impetigo. Ecthyma. Folliculitis. Furuncle (boil). Carbuncle. Cutaneous abscess. Cellulitis. Erysipelas. Staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome.
source_title: Standard Treatment Workflow (STW) for Bacterial Skin Infections
source_publisher: Department of Health Research, Ministry of Health and Family Welfare, Government of India

label: Dengue Warning Signs: Go to Hospital Immediately
text: Condition: Dengue Fever. Section: Dengue Warning Signs: Go to Hospital Immediately. Severe abdominal pain or tenderness. Persistent vomiting that does not stop. Bleeding from any site: black or tarry stools, bleeding gums, nosebleed, blood in urine, or unusual bruising. Fluid accumulation visible as swelling of the abdomen or difficulty breathing due to fluid around the lungs. Liver enlargement (swollen or tender abdomen on the right side). Signs of shock: weak and rapid pulse, cold and clammy skin, extreme restlessness or sudden fatigue, low blood pressure. Decreased or no urine output for several hours. Sudden drop in fever combined with worsening of general condition, this is a dangerous phase in dengue. Confusion, altered behaviour, or loss of consciousness.
source_title: Standard Treatment Workflow (STW) for the Management of Dengue Fever
source_publisher: Department of Health Research, Ministry of Health and Family Welfare, Government of India

label: Self-Care at Home for Dengue Without Warning Signs
text: Condition: Dengue Fever. Section: Self-Care at Home for Dengue Without Warning Signs. Rest completely, do not attempt to go to work or school. Drink plenty of fluids: water, ORS, coconut water, fruit juices, soups, dengue causes significant fluid loss. Take paracetamol for fever only, do not take aspirin, ibuprofen, or other NSAIDs as these increase the risk of bleeding in dengue. Apply a cold compress or sponge with lukewarm water for high fever. Monitor closely for any warning sign listed above, if any appear, go to hospital immediately. Daily monitoring is essential even at home: check if the person can drink fluids, passes urine, and has no new bleeding. Protect the patient from further mosquito bites to prevent spreading dengue to others, use mosquito nets and repellents. Do not self-medicate with any anti-inflammatory or blood-thinning medicines.
source_title: Standard Treatment Workflow (STW) for the Management of Dengue Fever
source_publisher: Department of Health Research, Ministry of Health and Family Welfare, Government of India

label: See a Doctor on the Same Day
text: Condition: Dengue Fever. Section: See a Doctor on the Same Day. Fever with severe headache, pain behind the eyes, and body aches, especially in a dengue-prone area or after recent travel. Fever with a skin rash. Fever that persists beyond 2 to 3 days without improvement. Fever suddenly dropping but the person feeling worse, this is a critical phase requiring monitoring. Any dengue fever in a child, elderly person, pregnant woman, or someone with diabetes, heart disease, or kidney disease, these groups are at higher risk of severe dengue.
source_title: Standard Treatment Workflow (STW) for the Management of Dengue Fever
source_publisher: Department of Health Research, Ministry of Health and Family Welfare, Government of India

label: Go to Hospital Without Delay
text: Condition: Dengue Fever. Section: Go to Hospital Without Delay. Any warning sign listed above, severe abdominal pain, persistent vomiting, bleeding, signs of shock, confusion, no urine output. Dengue with suspected shock: cold extremities, restlessness, weak pulse. Dengue with active bleeding from any site. Dengue with severe difficulty breathing. Dengue with impaired consciousness.
source_title: Standard Treatment Workflow (STW) for the Management of Dengue Fever
source_publisher: Department of Health Research, Ministry of Health and Family Welfare, Government of India

label: Condition Overview
text: Condition: Dengue Fever. Section: Condition Overview. Dengue is a mosquito-borne viral fever. Suspect dengue if a person has fever and two or more of the following: nausea, vomiting, rash, muscle pain, headache, pain behind the eyes, joint pain, or unusual bleeding, especially if they live in or recently travelled to a dengue-prone area.
source_title: Standard Treatment Workflow (STW) for the Management of Dengue Fever
source_publisher: Department of Health Research, Ministry of Health and Family Welfare, Government of India

label: Critical Note
text: Condition: Dengue Fever. Section: Critical Note. Dengue must be managed under medical supervision with daily monitoring of blood counts and clinical status. Do not treat dengue at home beyond basic supportive care. The transition from mild to severe dengue can happen quickly.
source_title: Standard Treatment Workflow (STW) for the Management of Dengue Fever
source_publisher: Department of Health Research, Ministry of Health and Family Welfare, Government of India

label: Signs That Need Specialist Attention
text: Condition: Dermatophytosis (Ringworm / Fungal Skin Infection). Section: Signs That Need Specialist Attention. Very extensive infection covering large areas of the body. No improvement at all after 4 weeks of regular treatment. Infection that keeps coming back repeatedly despite completing full treatment. Infection present during pregnancy or in someone with liver, kidney, or heart disease. Suspected or known history of prolonged use of steroid-containing creams, these can significantly worsen fungal infections and make them very difficult to treat.
source_title: Standard Treatment Workflow (STW) for Dermatophytoses
source_publisher: Department of Health Research, Ministry of Health and Family Welfare, Government of India

label: Self-Care at Home
text: Condition: Dermatophytosis (Ringworm / Fungal Skin Infection). Section: Self-Care at Home. Take a daily bath with regular soap and normal temperature water. Dry the skin thoroughly after bathing, especially the area between the toes and skin folds. Wash clothes separately in hot water and dry them inside-out in the sun. Do not share towels, clothes, or undergarments with others. Do not re-wear clothes before washing them. Keep nails trimmed short, infected nails are fragile and can spread the fungus. Avoid walking barefoot in public places such as swimming pools or community bathing areas. Wear cotton socks and change them daily. Do not use any steroid-containing cream (often sold as combination creams at chemists), these make fungal infections much worse. Do not stop treatment as soon as the itching improves, always complete the full course as the infection is still present. Do not self-medicate; this can make the infection harder to treat later.
source_title: Standard Treatment Workflow (STW) for Dermatophytoses
source_publisher: Department of Health Research, Ministry of Health and Family Welfare, Government of India

label: See a Doctor
text: Condition: Dermatophytosis (Ringworm / Fungal Skin Infection). Section: See a Doctor. Any itchy, ring-shaped, scaly rash on the skin, groin, feet, or hands. Nail discoloration, thickening, or crumbling. Infection that has not responded to treatment after 4 weeks. Infection spreading to other family members. Infection in the groin, palms, or soles. Scaling along the creases of palms or soles, or dried blisters on feet. If you are pregnant or have a chronic illness before starting any treatment.
source_title: Standard Treatment Workflow (STW) for Dermatophytoses
source_publisher: Department of Health Research, Ministry of Health and Family Welfare, Government of India

label: Refer to Specialist or Tertiary Centre
text: Condition: Dermatophytosis (Ringworm / Fungal Skin Infection). Section: Refer to Specialist or Tertiary Centre. Very extensive body-wide disease. No improvement after 4 weeks of regular treatment with correct antifungals. Infection not clearing despite prolonged treatment and good compliance. Recurrent infection. Presence of conditions that affect treatment choices: pregnancy, liver disease, kidney disease, or heart disease.
source_title: Standard Treatment Workflow (STW) for Dermatophytoses
source_publisher: Department of Health Research, Ministry of Health and Family Welfare, Government of India

label: Types Covered
text: Condition: Dermatophytosis (Ringworm / Fungal Skin Infection). Section: Types Covered. Tinea corporis (ringworm on body). Tinea cruris (groin area). Tinea pedis (athlete's foot). Tinea manuum (hands). Onychomycosis (nail infection).
source_title: Standard Treatment Workflow (STW) for Dermatophytoses
source_publisher: Department of Health Research, Ministry of Health and Family Welfare, Government of India

condition: Diabetes (Type 2): Awareness, Symptoms, and When to Seek Care
label: Diabetic Emergency Signs: Go to Hospital Immediately
text: Condition: Diabetes (Type 2): Awareness, Symptoms, and When to Seek Care. Section: Diabetic Emergency Signs: Go to Hospital Immediately. Hypoglycaemia (low blood sugar), symptoms: trembling or shaking, sudden sweating, anxiety or irritability, confusion, fast heartbeat, dizziness, blurred vision, weakness, seizures, or unconsciousness. These can occur if a person with diabetes skips meals or takes too much diabetes medicine. Immediate action: if the person is conscious and able to swallow, give sugar immediately, loose sugar, a sweet biscuit, misri (rock candy), or any sweet drink. If unconscious, do not give anything by mouth, go to hospital immediately. Very high blood sugar with confusion, rapid breathing, and extreme thirst, may indicate diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA), which is a medical emergency. Chest pain or severe breathlessness in a person with diabetes, diabetes significantly increases the risk of heart attack. Stroke warning signs in a person with diabetes: sudden one-sided weakness, speech difficulty, severe headache, vision loss, go to hospital immediately. Non-healing wound or foot ulcer with spreading redness, swelling, pus, or bad smell, diabetic foot infections can become life-threatening quickly.
source_title: Standard Treatment Workflow (STW) for Diabetes Mellitus Type 2
source_publisher: Department of Health Research, Ministry of Health and Family Welfare, Government of India

condition: Diabetes (Type 2): Awareness, Symptoms, and When to Seek Care
label: Diabetic Emergency Signs: Go to Hospital Immediately
text: Condition: Diabetes (Type 2): Awareness, Symptoms, and When to Seek Care. Section: Diabetic Emergency Signs: Go to Hospital Immediately. High fever with severe infection signs in a diabetic person, diabetes worsens the severity of infections.
source_title: Standard Treatment Workflow (STW) for Diabetes Mellitus Type 2
source_publisher: Department of Health Research, Ministry of Health and Family Welfare, Government of India

condition: Diabetes (Type 2): Awareness, Symptoms, and When to Seek Care
label: Daily Self-Care for Persons with Diabetes
text: Condition: Diabetes (Type 2): Awareness, Symptoms, and When to Seek Care. Section: Daily Self-Care for Persons with Diabetes. Take your diabetes medicines exactly as prescribed by your doctor, do not stop or change the dose on your own. Eat regular meals at consistent times, skipping meals can cause low blood sugar in those on certain diabetes medicines. Always carry something sweet (sugar, misri, a biscuit) in case of low blood sugar symptoms. Follow a diet low in refined sugar, white rice, maida, and sweet drinks. Eat more vegetables, whole grains, pulses, and fruits in moderate amounts. Be physically active, at least 30 minutes of walking or light exercise daily helps control blood sugar. Do not smoke, smoking dramatically increases the risk of heart attack and kidney damage in diabetics. Avoid alcohol or use it very minimally. Inspect your feet every day for cuts, blisters, redness, swelling, or wounds, even small injuries can become serious in diabetics. Wear proper footwear at all times, avoid going barefoot. Monitor your blood sugar regularly as advised by your doctor.
source_title: Standard Treatment Workflow (STW) for Diabetes Mellitus Type 2
source_publisher: Department of Health Research, Ministry of Health and Family Welfare, Government of India

condition: Diabetes (Type 2): Awareness, Symptoms, and When to Seek Care
label: Daily Self-Care for Persons with Diabetes
text: Condition: Diabetes (Type 2): Awareness, Symptoms, and When to Seek Care. Section: Daily Self-Care for Persons with Diabetes. Keep all follow-up appointments, diabetes requires regular monitoring of blood sugar, blood pressure, kidney function, and eyes.
source_title: Standard Treatment Workflow (STW) for Diabetes Mellitus Type 2
source_publisher: Department of Health Research, Ministry of Health and Family Welfare, Government of India

condition: Diabetes (Type 2): Awareness, Symptoms, and When to Seek Care
label: See a Doctor
text: Condition: Diabetes (Type 2): Awareness, Symptoms, and When to Seek Care. Section: See a Doctor. Symptoms that may suggest undiagnosed diabetes: frequent urination, excessive thirst, increased hunger, unexplained weight loss, extreme tiredness, blurred vision, slow-healing wounds, or recurring infections. Blood sugar reading on a home glucometer that is consistently high. Any person above 30 years of age who is overweight, has a family history of diabetes, or has high blood pressure, they should be screened annually. Any wound or cut on the foot in a diabetic that is not healing within a few days. Recurring infections: skin infections, fungal infections, urinary infections, or oral thrush in a person not known to be diabetic. A diabetic person whose blood sugar is not well controlled despite following advice. A diabetic person starting any new illness, even a common cold or fever needs closer monitoring.
source_title: Standard Treatment Workflow (STW) for Diabetes Mellitus Type 2
source_publisher: Department of Health Research, Ministry of Health and Family Welfare, Government of India

condition: Diabetes (Type 2): Awareness, Symptoms, and When to Seek Care
label: Go to Hospital Without Delay
text: Condition: Diabetes (Type 2): Awareness, Symptoms, and When to Seek Care. Section: Go to Hospital Without Delay. Any emergency danger sign listed above, hypoglycaemia with unconsciousness, chest pain, stroke signs, severe infection, spreading foot wound. A diabetic person who is very unwell, confused, or unable to eat or drink. Diabetic foot ulcer with spreading redness or foul smell, this requires urgent specialist care to prevent amputation. A diabetic with very high or very low blood sugar readings and symptoms.
source_title: Standard Treatment Workflow (STW) for Diabetes Mellitus Type 2
source_publisher: Department of Health Research, Ministry of Health and Family Welfare, Government of India

condition: Diabetes (Type 2): Awareness, Symptoms, and When to Seek Care
label: Who Should Be Screened for Diabetes
text: Condition: Diabetes (Type 2): Awareness, Symptoms, and When to Seek Care. Section: Who Should Be Screened for Diabetes. All adults above 30 years of age, at least once a year. Anyone who is overweight or obese. Anyone with a first-degree relative (parent or sibling) with diabetes. Anyone with high blood pressure or high cholesterol. Women with a history of diabetes during pregnancy (gestational diabetes). Anyone with symptoms: frequent urination, excessive thirst, unexplained weight loss, repeated infections, or slow-healing wounds.
source_title: Standard Treatment Workflow (STW) for Diabetes Mellitus Type 2
source_publisher: Department of Health Research, Ministry of Health and Family Welfare, Government of India

label: Scope Note
text: Condition: Diabetes (Type 2): Awareness, Symptoms, and When to Seek Care. Section: Scope Note. AIRA covers diabetes awareness, symptom recognition, and triage only. Diabetes management, medication, and dose advice must come from a doctor.

label: Signs That Need Urgent Medical Attention
text: Condition: Eczema / Dermatitis. Section: Signs That Need Urgent Medical Attention. Eczema with pus discharge, yellow crusting, or increasing warmth, this indicates a secondary bacterial infection. Widespread skin involvement with blistering or skin breakdown. Eczema associated with fever. Severe eczema covering large parts of the body that is not responding to any treatment.
source_title: Standard Treatment Workflow (STW) for Eczema / Dermatitis
source_publisher: Department of Health Research, Ministry of Health and Family Welfare, Government of India

label: Self-Care at Home
text: Condition: Eczema / Dermatitis. Section: Self-Care at Home. Apply a moisturiser immediately after bathing while the skin is still slightly damp, this is the most important step in managing eczema. Apply moisturiser multiple times during the day, not just once. Bathe daily with a mild soap and normal temperature water; avoid hot water. Keep fingernails short to reduce damage from scratching. Avoid scratching, scratching worsens eczema and risks infection. Identify and avoid triggers: specific soaps, detergents, fabrics, plants, or foods that make the skin worse. Wear loose, cotton clothing to reduce irritation. Avoid high-risk occupational exposures if possible: agricultural work, construction, hairdressing involve frequent skin contact with irritants. For contact dermatitis, identify and remove the cause (e.g. a specific soap, metal, or plant). Atopic dermatitis is often worse in winter, extra moisturising is important in cold weather. Do not use any steroid creams on your own without a doctor's guidance, especially on the face or skin folds.
source_title: Standard Treatment Workflow (STW) for Eczema / Dermatitis
source_publisher: Department of Health Research, Ministry of Health and Family Welfare, Government of India

label: See a Doctor
text: Condition: Eczema / Dermatitis. Section: See a Doctor. Any new rash with redness, scaling, or itching that is not improving within a week of basic care. Eczema on the face, eyelids, or genitals. Rash that you suspect may be caused by an allergen or irritant at work. Eczema that keeps recurring in the same areas. Skin that has become thickened or leathery in patches from long-standing eczema. Eczema with signs of infection: pus, yellow crust, or increasing redness. Eczema in a child, particularly if involving the face, skin folds, or causing disturbed sleep from itching.
source_title: Standard Treatment Workflow (STW) for Eczema / Dermatitis
source_publisher: Department of Health Research, Ministry of Health and Family Welfare, Government of India

label: Refer to Higher Centre
text: Condition: Eczema / Dermatitis. Section: Refer to Higher Centre. Severe eczema not responding to treatment at the primary care level. Widespread disease requiring phototherapy or systemic treatment. Suspected allergic contact dermatitis where patch testing is needed to identify the allergen. Unusual presentations that may be mistaken for eczema: psoriasis, fungal infection, or cutaneous lymphoma.
source_title: Standard Treatment Workflow (STW) for Eczema / Dermatitis
source_publisher: Department of Health Research, Ministry of Health and Family Welfare, Government of India

label: Types Covered
text: Condition: Eczema / Dermatitis. Section: Types Covered. Atopic dermatitis. Contact dermatitis (allergic and irritant). Seborrhoeic dermatitis. Nummular eczema. Venous eczema. Hand eczema.
source_title: Standard Treatment Workflow (STW) for Eczema / Dermatitis
source_publisher: Department of Health Research, Ministry of Health and Family Welfare, Government of India

label: Red Flag Signs: Go to Hospital
text: Condition: Epistaxis (Nosebleed). Section: Red Flag Signs: Go to Hospital. Nosebleed that does not stop after 20 minutes of correct first aid. Nosebleed with very heavy or rapid blood loss causing dizziness, weakness, or faintness. Nosebleed only from one side of the nose persistently, without a clear cause like trauma, this may need investigation. Nosebleed with nasal blockage, a visible mass, or changes in vision or the eye, could indicate a serious nasal or sinus condition. Nosebleed in a person on blood thinners or with a known bleeding disorder. Nosebleed in a person with uncontrolled high blood pressure. Nosebleed in a person after head trauma. Nosebleed with bleeding from other sites at the same time, gums, skin bruising, blood in urine or stool, may indicate a blood disorder. Recurrent, profuse nosebleeds in a teenage boy, requires specialist evaluation.
source_title: Standard Treatment Workflow (STW) for the Management of Epistaxis
source_publisher: Department of Health Research, Ministry of Health and Family Welfare, Government of India

label: First Aid for Nosebleed at Home
text: Condition: Epistaxis (Nosebleed). Section: First Aid for Nosebleed at Home. Sit upright and lean slightly forward, do not tilt the head back, as this causes blood to flow down the throat and may cause vomiting or choking. Breathe through your mouth. Pinch the soft part of the nose (just below the bony bridge) firmly with your thumb and index finger, this is called Trotter's position. Hold the nose pinched continuously for 10 minutes without releasing, use a clock to time it, as most people underestimate the time. Apply a cold compress or ice wrapped in a cloth to the nose and cheeks. After 10 minutes, gently release and check if bleeding has stopped. If bleeding continues, repeat the pinching for another 10 minutes. Avoid blowing the nose forcefully immediately after the bleeding stops. Avoid hot drinks, physical exertion, and bending over for several hours after a nosebleed. Apply a small amount of petroleum jelly or liquid paraffin inside the nostril daily if you get recurrent nosebleeds due to dry air, this helps keep the mucosa moist.
source_title: Standard Treatment Workflow (STW) for the Management of Epistaxis
source_publisher: Department of Health Research, Ministry of Health and Family Welfare, Government of India

label: First Aid for Nosebleed at Home
text: Condition: Epistaxis (Nosebleed). Section: First Aid for Nosebleed at Home. Most nosebleeds in children are from the front of the nose (Little's area) due to dry air or nose picking and stop quickly with simple pressure.
source_title: Standard Treatment Workflow (STW) for the Management of Epistaxis
source_publisher: Department of Health Research, Ministry of Health and Family Welfare, Government of India

label: See a Doctor
text: Condition: Epistaxis (Nosebleed). Section: See a Doctor. Nosebleed that stopped but recurs frequently. Known high blood pressure with recurring nosebleeds, blood pressure needs to be checked and controlled. Nosebleed in a person with diabetes. Nosebleed in a child that keeps coming back despite no obvious cause.
source_title: Standard Treatment Workflow (STW) for the Management of Epistaxis
source_publisher: Department of Health Research, Ministry of Health and Family Welfare, Government of India

label: Go to Hospital Without Delay
text: Condition: Epistaxis (Nosebleed). Section: Go to Hospital Without Delay. Nosebleed not stopping after 20 minutes of sustained pressure. Heavy blood loss with dizziness, weakness, or rapid pulse. Nosebleed following a head injury. Nosebleed with associated bleeding from other sites. Nosebleed with one-sided nasal blockage, vision changes, or a visible swelling in the nose or face.
source_title: Standard Treatment Workflow (STW) for the Management of Epistaxis
source_publisher: Department of Health Research, Ministry of Health and Family Welfare, Government of India

label: Condition Overview
text: Condition: Epistaxis (Nosebleed). Section: Condition Overview. Epistaxis means bleeding from the nose. Most nosebleeds in adults are minor and related to dry air, nose picking, trauma, or uncontrolled blood pressure. Most can be managed at home with simple first aid.
source_title: Standard Treatment Workflow (STW) for the Management of Epistaxis
source_publisher: Department of Health Research, Ministry of Health and Family Welfare, Government of India

label: Red Flag Signs: Go to Hospital Immediately
text: Condition: Headache. Section: Red Flag Signs: Go to Hospital Immediately. The worst headache of your life, a sudden, extremely severe headache that reaches maximum intensity within seconds to minutes (thunderclap headache). This can be a sign of bleeding in the brain. First ever severe headache, especially in a person who does not usually get headaches. Headache with fever and stiff neck, may indicate meningitis. Headache with fever and change in behaviour, personality, or level of consciousness. Headache with confusion or disorientation. Headache with weakness, numbness, or paralysis on one side of the body or face. Headache with sudden vision changes or vision loss. Severe headache that wakes you up from sleep. Headache in a pregnant woman or someone who has recently given birth. New headache type in a person with cancer or a weakened immune system. Progressive headache that is steadily getting worse over days or weeks. Headache associated with a recent head injury.
source_title: Standard Treatment Workflow (STW) for the Management of Headache
source_publisher: Department of Health Research, Ministry of Health and Family Welfare, Government of India

label: Self-Care for Common Tension Headache or Known Migraine
text: Condition: Headache. Section: Self-Care for Common Tension Headache or Known Migraine. Rest in a quiet, dark, and cool room, this is especially helpful for migraine. Paracetamol can be taken for pain relief as per the dosage on the pack. Stay hydrated, dehydration is a common trigger for headaches. Apply a cold or warm compress to the forehead or the back of the neck. Avoid known personal triggers: irregular sleep, skipping meals, too much screen time, bright lights, strong smells, stress. Ensure at least 6 hours of sleep regularly, sleep deprivation is a major trigger for both tension headache and migraine. Reduce caffeine intake gradually if you consume large amounts, sudden stopping can also trigger headaches. Stress management: take short breaks, practice deep breathing, and avoid overwork. For migraine, lie down in a dark room and sleep if possible, sleep often relieves migraine. Do not take painkillers more than 3 days a week for headaches, overuse of painkillers causes its own rebound headaches.
source_title: Standard Treatment Workflow (STW) for the Management of Headache
source_publisher: Department of Health Research, Ministry of Health and Family Welfare, Government of India

label: See a Doctor
text: Condition: Headache. Section: See a Doctor. Headaches occurring more than twice a month. Headaches that are interfering with daily work or sleep. Headaches that are getting more frequent or more severe over time. Migraine not responding to paracetamol. Headache always on the same side of the head. Headache with nausea and vomiting regularly. Tension headache persisting for many years with significant sleep disturbance. Any new or unusual headache pattern that you have not had before.
source_title: Standard Treatment Workflow (STW) for the Management of Headache
source_publisher: Department of Health Research, Ministry of Health and Family Welfare, Government of India

label: Go to Hospital Without Delay
text: Condition: Headache. Section: Go to Hospital Without Delay. Any red flag sign listed above, thunderclap headache, fever with stiff neck, confusion, one-sided weakness, vision loss, worst headache of your life. Headache that is progressively worsening over days and not responding to any treatment. Headache with seizures or loss of consciousness. Headache in someone with a known cancer or on immunosuppressive drugs. Severe migraine with hemiplegia (arm or leg weakness on one side), vertigo, or significant visual impairment, these are atypical and need urgent evaluation to rule out stroke.
source_title: Standard Treatment Workflow (STW) for the Management of Headache
source_publisher: Department of Health Research, Ministry of Health and Family Welfare, Government of India

label: Types Covered
text: Condition: Headache. Section: Types Covered. Tension headache. Migraine. Cluster headache. Secondary headache due to serious underlying conditions.
source_title: Standard Treatment Workflow (STW) for the Management of Headache
source_publisher: Department of Health Research, Ministry of Health and Family Welfare, Government of India

condition: Hypertension (High Blood Pressure): Awareness, Symptoms, and When to Seek Care
label: Heart Attack Warning Signs: Call 112 or Go to Hospital Immediately
text: Condition: Hypertension (High Blood Pressure): Awareness, Symptoms, and When to Seek Care. Section: Heart Attack Warning Signs: Call 112 or Go to Hospital Immediately. Pain, pressure, or constriction in the centre of the chest lasting more than 30 minutes. Pain spreading to the jaw, neck, arms, shoulders, or back. Shortness of breath along with chest discomfort. Nausea with chest pain. Loss of consciousness.
source_title: Module for ASHA on Non-Communicable Diseases: Chapter 3: Hypertension
source_publisher: Ministry of Health and Family Welfare, Government of India / National Health Mission

condition: Hypertension (High Blood Pressure): Awareness, Symptoms, and When to Seek Care
label: Stroke Warning Signs: Call 112 or Go to Hospital Immediately
text: Condition: Hypertension (High Blood Pressure): Awareness, Symptoms, and When to Seek Care. Section: Stroke Warning Signs: Call 112 or Go to Hospital Immediately. Sudden weakness, paralysis, or numbness on one side of the face, arm, or leg. Loss of speech or sudden difficulty speaking or understanding speech. Dimness or loss of vision, particularly in one eye. Unexplained dizziness, unsteadiness, or sudden falls. Sudden severe headache or loss of consciousness. Any of these signs in a person with high blood pressure must be treated as a medical emergency, refer immediately to a Community Health Centre or hospital.
source_title: Module for ASHA on Non-Communicable Diseases: Chapter 3: Hypertension
source_publisher: Ministry of Health and Family Welfare, Government of India / National Health Mission

condition: Hypertension (High Blood Pressure): Awareness, Symptoms, and When to Seek Care
label: Lifestyle Measures for Persons with High Blood Pressure
text: Condition: Hypertension (High Blood Pressure): Awareness, Symptoms, and When to Seek Care. Section: Lifestyle Measures for Persons with High Blood Pressure. Stop all use of tobacco, smoking or chewing tobacco significantly raises blood pressure and risk of heart attack. Reduce alcohol intake. Reduce salt intake, limit to a maximum of 1 teaspoon (5 grams) of salt per day for the whole family. Reduce consumption of oily, fried, and fatty foods. Reduce intake of refined cereals (maida), sugar, and sweet beverages. Eat more fresh fruits, vegetables, whole grains, and whole pulses. Maintain a healthy weight, losing weight if overweight significantly reduces blood pressure. Be physically active, at least 30 minutes of brisk walking or moderate activity daily. Manage stress, practice relaxation techniques, take breaks, maintain social connections. Take blood pressure medicines every day as prescribed, do not stop on your own even if you feel fine. Get blood pressure checked at least once a month if on treatment. Attend regular follow-up at the Primary Health Centre or sub-centre as advised.
source_title: Module for ASHA on Non-Communicable Diseases: Chapter 3: Hypertension
source_publisher: Ministry of Health and Family Welfare, Government of India / National Health Mission

condition: Hypertension (High Blood Pressure): Awareness, Symptoms, and When to Seek Care
label: See a Doctor
text: Condition: Hypertension (High Blood Pressure): Awareness, Symptoms, and When to Seek Care. Section: See a Doctor. Hypertension is called the silent killer because it usually has no symptoms, the only way to detect it is to measure blood pressure. All adults aged 30 years and above should have their blood pressure checked at least once a year even if they feel well. A blood pressure reading of 140 mm Hg systolic (upper number) or 90 mm Hg diastolic (lower number) or above on a single reading should prompt referral to a medical officer for confirmation and further management. Frequent headaches, especially at the back of the head in the morning, can sometimes be a symptom of very high blood pressure. Any person with high blood pressure who develops a new symptom or illness, they are at higher risk of complications. Family history of heart attack or stroke, screening and prevention are very important.
source_title: Module for ASHA on Non-Communicable Diseases: Chapter 3: Hypertension
source_publisher: Ministry of Health and Family Welfare, Government of India / National Health Mission

condition: Hypertension (High Blood Pressure): Awareness, Symptoms, and When to Seek Care
label: Go to Hospital Without Delay
text: Condition: Hypertension (High Blood Pressure): Awareness, Symptoms, and When to Seek Care. Section: Go to Hospital Without Delay. Any heart attack or stroke warning sign listed above, these are medical emergencies. Very severe headache with high blood pressure and visual disturbance or confusion, may indicate hypertensive emergency. A known hypertensive patient who has stopped their medication and is now feeling unwell. A hypertensive patient with chest pain, breathlessness, or swelling of the legs, may indicate heart failure.
source_title: Module for ASHA on Non-Communicable Diseases: Chapter 3: Hypertension
source_publisher: Ministry of Health and Family Welfare, Government of India / National Health Mission

condition: Hypertension (High Blood Pressure): Awareness, Symptoms, and When to Seek Care
label: Preventing Heart Attack and Stroke in Hypertensive Patients
text: Condition: Hypertension (High Blood Pressure): Awareness, Symptoms, and When to Seek Care. Section: Preventing Heart Attack and Stroke in Hypertensive Patients. All adults above 30 years should be screened annually for both high blood pressure and diabetes. Blood pressure and blood sugar must be monitored regularly in high-risk individuals, those with a family history of heart attack or stroke. Anyone who experiences heart attack or stroke warning signs must seek immediate medical care, every minute matters.
source_title: Module for ASHA on Non-Communicable Diseases: Chapter 3: Hypertension
source_publisher: Ministry of Health and Family Welfare, Government of India / National Health Mission

condition: Hypertension (High Blood Pressure): Awareness, Symptoms, and When to Seek Care
label: Scope Note
text: Condition: Hypertension (High Blood Pressure): Awareness, Symptoms, and When to Seek Care. Section: Scope Note. AIRA covers hypertension awareness, warning signs, lifestyle measures, and triage only. Diagnosis and treatment must be done by a qualified doctor or medical officer.
source_title: Module for ASHA on Non-Communicable Diseases: Chapter 3: Hypertension
source_publisher: Ministry of Health and Family Welfare, Government of India / National Health Mission

label: Red Flag Signs: Go to Hospital Immediately
text: Condition: Sore Throat and Pharyngitis. Section: Red Flag Signs: Go to Hospital Immediately. Sore throat with high fever, drooling of saliva, and difficulty or inability to swallow, this may indicate epiglottitis or a deep neck infection, which can close the airway. Breathing difficulty or noisy breathing with a sore throat. Muffled or hot potato voice (very thick, muffled speech) with sore throat. Swelling of the throat visible from outside the neck. One tonsil significantly larger than the other, especially with severe throat pain and fever, may be a peritonsillar abscess. White or grey membrane in the throat that extends beyond the tonsils with a very unwell appearance, may be diphtheria. Sore throat with generalised swollen glands across the body (neck, armpits, groin) and feeling very unwell. Sore throat with new cardiac symptoms or joint swelling after recovery, may suggest rheumatic fever, a complication of streptococcal infection.
source_title: Standard Treatment Workflow (STW) for the Management of Pharyngitis and Sore Throat
source_publisher: Department of Health Research, Ministry of Health and Family Welfare, Government of India

label: Self-Care at Home for Mild Sore Throat
text: Condition: Sore Throat and Pharyngitis. Section: Self-Care at Home for Mild Sore Throat. Gargle with warm salt water several times a day, dissolve half a teaspoon of salt in a glass of warm water and gargle for 30 seconds. This reduces swelling and kills surface bacteria. Drink warm liquids: warm water, warm water with honey and ginger, warm soups, warm herbal teas. Rest your voice and avoid shouting or excessive talking. Paracetamol or ibuprofen can be taken for pain relief as directed on the pack. Avoid very cold drinks and ice cream if they worsen the pain. Avoid smoking and exposure to tobacco smoke, smoke irritates the throat and slows healing. Address GERD (acid reflux) if it is a known issue, acid coming back up is a common cause of throat irritation. Most viral sore throats resolve on their own within 7 to 10 days with home care. Do not demand or self-purchase antibiotics for a sore throat, most sore throats are viral and antibiotics will not help.
source_title: Standard Treatment Workflow (STW) for the Management of Pharyngitis and Sore Throat
source_publisher: Department of Health Research, Ministry of Health and Family Welfare, Government of India

label: See a Doctor
text: Condition: Sore Throat and Pharyngitis. Section: See a Doctor. Sore throat with high fever (above 38.5 degrees Celsius) and swollen, tender glands in the neck. Pus or white spots visible on the tonsils. Sore throat that is not improving after 5 to 7 days of home care. Throat pain that is severe enough to make swallowing very difficult. Sore throat with ear pain. Recurring sore throats or tonsillitis (more than 5 episodes a year). Sore throat in a person with a history of rheumatic fever or rheumatic heart disease, streptococcal throat infection can trigger a relapse. Sore throat with runny nose, cough, and red eyes, likely a viral infection but should be assessed if it is severe.
source_title: Standard Treatment Workflow (STW) for the Management of Pharyngitis and Sore Throat
source_publisher: Department of Health Research, Ministry of Health and Family Welfare, Government of India

label: Go to Hospital Without Delay
text: Condition: Sore Throat and Pharyngitis. Section: Go to Hospital Without Delay. Any red flag sign listed above, drooling, breathing difficulty, muffled voice, single very swollen tonsil, throat membrane, inability to open the mouth. Suspected epiglottitis or deep neck space infection, these can close the airway rapidly. Suspected diphtheria in a child who is unvaccinated or incompletely vaccinated. Complications after a sore throat: new swelling in the neck, inability to open mouth, high fever returning after initial improvement.
source_title: Standard Treatment Workflow (STW) for the Management of Pharyngitis and Sore Throat
source_publisher: Department of Health Research, Ministry of Health and Family Welfare, Government of India

label: Condition Overview
text: Condition: Sore Throat and Pharyngitis. Section: Condition Overview. Sore throat is pain in the throat on swallowing. It may be caused by a virus (most common) or bacteria. Viral sore throats do not need antibiotics. Bacterial sore throat (streptococcal) has specific features and needs a doctor to decide on treatment.
source_title: Standard Treatment Workflow (STW) for the Management of Pharyngitis and Sore Throat
source_publisher: Department of Health Research, Ministry of Health and Family Welfare, Government of India

label: Signs of Severe or Complicated Scabies: See a Doctor
text: Condition: Scabies. Section: Signs of Severe or Complicated Scabies: See a Doctor. Crusted (Norwegian) scabies: thick, yellow-brown crusts on the skin, particularly on the hands and feet, this is a severe form seen in people with weak immunity and is highly contagious. Signs of secondary bacterial infection: skin that is red, swollen, warm, and has pus or a foul smell. Scabies in someone who is immunocompromised (on steroids, with HIV, or on chemotherapy), this can become very severe quickly. Widespread scabies outbreak in a school, orphanage, or shared-living setting.
source_title: Standard Treatment Workflow (STW) for Scabies
source_publisher: Department of Health Research, Ministry of Health and Family Welfare, Government of India

label: Self-Care and Household Measures
text: Condition: Scabies. Section: Self-Care and Household Measures. All family members and close physical contacts must be treated at the same time, even if they have no symptoms, treating only the affected person will lead to re-infestation. Wash all clothes, towels, and bedlinen used in the past three days in hot water and dry them in the sun. Items that cannot be washed (shoes, bags) can be sealed in a plastic bag for at least 3 days, the mite cannot survive without human contact. Do not share clothing, towels, or bedding with others during the infestation. Maintain good general hygiene throughout treatment. Important: itching can continue for several weeks after successful treatment, this is normal and does not mean the treatment has failed. Do not repeat the treatment application just because itching continues, continue antihistamines for relief instead. If new lesions appear or itching continues for more than 3 to 4 weeks after treatment, re-infestation is likely, this usually means a close contact was not treated.
source_title: Standard Treatment Workflow (STW) for Scabies
source_publisher: Department of Health Research, Ministry of Health and Family Welfare, Government of India

label: See a Doctor
text: Condition: Scabies. Section: See a Doctor. Intense itching that is worse at night, especially in the fingers, wrists, belly button area, breasts, buttocks, or genitals. Other family members developing the same symptoms. Small, red, itchy bumps or burrow marks between the fingers or on the wrists. Itching and rash with no obvious cause in a child. Persistent itching and new lesions after completing a course of treatment. Any sign of secondary skin infection (pus, crusting, fever).
source_title: Standard Treatment Workflow (STW) for Scabies
source_publisher: Department of Health Research, Ministry of Health and Family Welfare, Government of India

label: Refer to Higher Centre
text: Condition: Scabies. Section: Refer to Higher Centre. Crusted (Norwegian) scabies, requires specialised treatment and isolation precautions. Scabies in an immunocompromised person. Secondary bacterial infection that is spreading or not responding to treatment. Persistent, treatment-resistant nodular lesions over the genitals.
source_title: Standard Treatment Workflow (STW) for Scabies
source_publisher: Department of Health Research, Ministry of Health and Family Welfare, Government of India

label: Red Flag Signs: Go to Hospital Immediately
text: Condition: Urinary Tract Infection (UTI). Section: Red Flag Signs: Go to Hospital Immediately. Fever above 100 degrees Fahrenheit along with urinary symptoms. Chills and rigors (shaking with cold). Fast heart rate (tachycardia). Fast breathing (tachypnoea). Low blood pressure (hypotension). Pain or tenderness in the flank (the side of the back, just below the ribs), this may indicate a kidney infection. Confusion or altered mental state (obtundation). Signs of sepsis: high fever, fast heart rate, very unwell appearance, confusion.
source_title: Standard Treatment Workflow (STW) for Urinary Tract Infections
source_publisher: Department of Health Research, Ministry of Health and Family Welfare, Government of India

label: Supportive Self-Care While Seeking Medical Help
text: Condition: Urinary Tract Infection (UTI). Section: Supportive Self-Care While Seeking Medical Help. Drink plenty of water and fluids to flush out the urinary tract. Do not delay seeking a doctor. UTIs require antibiotic treatment prescribed by a doctor and should not be managed with home remedies alone. Paracetamol can be taken for pain relief while waiting to see a doctor. Avoid holding urine for long periods. Empty your bladder fully each time you urinate. Wipe from front to back after using the toilet (for women) to avoid introducing bacteria. Urinate soon after sexual intercourse to help prevent UTIs.
source_title: Standard Treatment Workflow (STW) for Urinary Tract Infections
source_publisher: Department of Health Research, Ministry of Health and Family Welfare, Government of India

label: See a Doctor Promptly
text: Condition: Urinary Tract Infection (UTI). Section: See a Doctor Promptly. Burning or pain when urinating. Frequent urge to urinate even when little urine passes. Feeling of urgency, needing to rush to the toilet. Pain or pressure in the lower abdomen or pelvis. Cloudy, dark, or foul-smelling urine. Blood in the urine. Urinary symptoms in a pregnant woman. UTI in pregnancy requires prompt treatment. Urinary symptoms in a person with diabetes, kidney disease, or a known urinary tract abnormality, these are high-risk groups. Recurrent UTIs (more than 2 in 6 months or 3 in a year). Symptoms not improving after a full course of prescribed antibiotics.
source_title: Standard Treatment Workflow (STW) for Urinary Tract Infections
source_publisher: Department of Health Research, Ministry of Health and Family Welfare, Government of India

label: Refer to Higher Centre
text: Condition: Urinary Tract Infection (UTI). Section: Refer to Higher Centre. Any red flag sign is present, fever, chills, flank pain, fast heartbeat, low blood pressure. Signs of kidney infection (pyelonephritis): fever, flank pain, very unwell. UTI in pregnancy that is complicated or not responding to first treatment. Recent urological procedure or surgery with new urinary symptoms. Recurrent UTI requiring investigation (cystoscopy or urodynamics). UTI in a person with known kidney stones or urinary tract obstruction. Prostatitis: UTI symptoms combined with pelvic pain or a tender prostate in men.
source_title: Standard Treatment Workflow (STW) for Urinary Tract Infections
source_publisher: Department of Health Research, Ministry of Health and Family Welfare, Government of India

label: High Risk Groups
text: Condition: Urinary Tract Infection (UTI). Section: High Risk Groups. Pregnant women. People with kidney stones. People with urinary tract obstruction or anatomical abnormality. People who are immunocompromised. People with chronic kidney disease. People who have recently had a urological procedure.
source_title: Standard Treatment Workflow (STW) for Urinary Tract Infections
source_publisher: Department of Health Research, Ministry of Health and Family Welfare, Government of India

label: Types Covered
text: Condition: Urinary Tract Infection (UTI). Section: Types Covered. Uncomplicated UTI (bladder infection). Complicated UTI / Pyelonephritis (kidney infection). Recurrent UTI.
source_title: Standard Treatment Workflow (STW) for Urinary Tract Infections
source_publisher: Department of Health Research, Ministry of Health and Family Welfare, Government of India

label: Emergency Signs: Call 112 or Go to Hospital Immediately
text: Condition: Urticaria (Hives) and Angioedema. Section: Emergency Signs: Call 112 or Go to Hospital Immediately. Swelling of the lips, tongue, or throat. Difficulty breathing, choking, or shortness of breath. Hoarse voice or difficulty speaking after swelling. Swelling of the airway (laryngeal angioedema), this is a life-threatening emergency. Respiratory distress combined with hives, this may indicate anaphylaxis. Shock: dizziness, loss of consciousness, very low blood pressure after exposure to an allergen.
source_title: Standard Treatment Workflow (STW) for Urticaria and Angioedema
source_publisher: Department of Health Research, Ministry of Health and Family Welfare, Government of India

label: Self-Care at Home for Mild Urticaria
text: Condition: Urticaria (Hives) and Angioedema. Section: Self-Care at Home for Mild Urticaria. Mild hives that are itchy but not affecting breathing can often be managed with an antihistamine prescribed by a doctor. Identify and avoid triggers: common triggers include certain foods, medicines (especially pain relievers like NSAIDs), insect stings, latex, and stress. Avoid common drug triggers if you have a history of urticaria: pain relievers such as ibuprofen or aspirin can trigger or worsen hives in some people, always inform your doctor of your history. Apply a cool compress to itchy areas for temporary relief. Wear loose, cool clothing to reduce skin irritation. Avoid vigorous exercise if exercise is a known trigger for your urticaria. Urticaria that resolves within 24 hours and does not recur may not need further treatment, reassurance is appropriate. About half of chronic urticaria cases resolve on their own within 12 to 24 months. Do not stop antihistamines abruptly if a doctor has prescribed a prolonged course.
source_title: Standard Treatment Workflow (STW) for Urticaria and Angioedema
source_publisher: Department of Health Research, Ministry of Health and Family Welfare, Government of India

label: See a Doctor
text: Condition: Urticaria (Hives) and Angioedema. Section: See a Doctor. Hives that appear repeatedly over several days or are not going away. Any swelling of the face, lips, or eyes even without breathing difficulty. Urticaria lasting more than 6 weeks, this is chronic urticaria and needs evaluation. Hives that last longer than 24 to 48 hours in one spot, are painful, and leave bruising, this may be urticarial vasculitis, which is different from ordinary hives. Hives that seem related to a specific food, drug, or situation, allergy testing may be needed. Urticaria that is not improving with antihistamines. Urticaria associated with joint pain, fever, or feeling generally unwell.
source_title: Standard Treatment Workflow (STW) for Urticaria and Angioedema

label: Refer to Higher Centre
text: Condition: Urticaria (Hives) and Angioedema. Section: Refer to Higher Centre. Any breathing difficulty, throat swelling, or signs of anaphylaxis, refer after emergency stabilisation. Angioedema affecting the throat or airway. Urticaria not controlled by standard antihistamines even at higher doses. Unusual urticaria: welts lasting more than 24 to 48 hours with bruising. Angioedema without urticaria, this may indicate a rare hereditary condition (C1 inhibitor deficiency) that requires specialist investigation. Urticaria with associated systemic symptoms (fever, joint pain, weight loss).

label: Condition Overview
text: Condition: Urticaria (Hives) and Angioedema. Section: Condition Overview. Urticaria: Sudden appearance of raised, itchy welts (wheals) on the skin of variable size and shape, surrounded by redness. Individual welts usually resolve within 1 to 24 hours but new ones may keep appearing. Chronic urticaria means it has lasted more than 6 weeks. Angioedema: Sudden, deep swelling of the skin, often affecting the face, lips, tongue, throat, or genitals. It can take up to 72 hours to resolve. When it affects the throat or airway, it is a medical emergency.
